When Elizabeth and Tom Wilcox realised they could never afford to buy the home they wanted for themselves and their two children, they decided to take a leap of faith.
They'd find another couple with young kids, complete strangers to them, and propose that they go halves on a property and all move in together.
Based in Vancouver, which has long had some of the highest house prices in Canada, the Wilcoxes were desperate to buy a home that had a back garden for their children to play in.
"We wanted a house with a yard that could fit a trampoline, in a walkable neighbourhood, but we couldn't afford it," says Elizabeth, a project manager in the healthcare sector.
With a budget of C$1m ($700,000; £500,000) all they could hope for was a small apartment with a balcony at best.
That was when Elizabeth came up with the idea of buying with another family.
In 2023, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans co-bought a six-bedroom, detached house, complete with a back garden, for C$1.85m.

The two families split the deposit of C$250,000, and continue to go halves on the monthly mortgage payments of C$3,900. They also divide bills and other expenses equally, such as any necessary home repairs.
Elizabeth says the arrangement has saved both families "tens of thousands of dollars".
Image source, Elizabeth Wilcox Image caption, Mums Ashley Pullman, left, and Elizabeth Wilcox say the two families get along

While there is no official data available for the number of people buying homes with people they previously didn't know, Parimal Gosai says he has seen a big increase in interest in Toronto as a response to high property prices.
Gosai is the founder and CEO of Husmates, an app and website that connects people in Canada's largest city who are looking to potentially buy a home with a stranger.
It can be seen as "a financial relationship, and that takes emotions out of it", he says.

It's unclear how common this phenomenon is elsewhere in the world. David Hollingworth, from British mortgage broker L&C, says while he hasn't come across it himself, he thinks it also happens in the UK, though is "very niche".
"I remember that before Covid-19 there was a matchmaking event in a London pub, like speed dating, for people looking to buy a house with a stranger," he says. "How successful this was I don't know."
Image source, Elizabeth Wilcox Image caption, The Wilcoxes and the Pullmans pooled their resources to buy a detached Vancouver home
Three years on, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans say their living arrangement is still working out.
While each family has some private living spaces, such as their own kitchens, they share the big basement-level living room, which includes a home gym in one corner, and a shared freezer.
"If someone says they're in the basement to work out, we know not to go there for a bit, and it's never been an issue," says Elizabeth.
Ashley agrees that there are no problems. "Maybe it's arrogance but my husband and I felt like we were the type of people who could live with strangers," she says.

Image source, Getty Images By Imran Rahman-Jones Technology reporter Published 2 hours ago Outages and IT failings are commonplace - but not on this scale.

In the past week, there has been a massive Microsoft outage , an apparent tech glitch which grounded all US flights for hours , and issues for the National Security Agency (NSA). That's not to mention outages affecting the biggest US banks , as well as a major flaw found in a popular programming language .
These are all separate incidents - but the fact they have all come so close to each other has got people wondering if they might be linked.
There is no evidence to suggest this - but they do tell us a lot about how the modern tech world works, and where the vulnerabilities lie.
As is often the case, many outages were a result of an update or installation going wrong somewhere in a system.
A network upgrade at Microsoft caused servers to become overloaded and shut down.
It was also upgrades to a creaky old network which grounded thousands of planes in the US over the weekend.
Problems with the NSA's internal communication system and, separately, Apple's iCloud and Apple Pay were also blamed on things going wrong during system updates.
Disruption to payments in US banks has been put down to a "software bug" from JP Morgan Chase. The bank says it is not a cyber-security incident.
But some recent problems are in fact related to cyber-security vulnerabilities.
AI was used to discover flaws in Java, the third-most popular programming language in the world.
And researcher Scott Helme also discovered malicious code in Optimizely, a platform which is used by some of the world's largest companies.
Hackers were able to steal about $7,000 (£5,300) in cryptocurrency before they were discovered and kicked out.
Let's address the cyber incidents first - and the role of new AI models.
"I would be very surprised if all of these cyber-attacks and the attackers behind them were not using AI to accelerate themselves," Helme told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

Since the summer, AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI have decided it's too risky to give the general public access to the most advanced models before allowing certain companies and institutions to use them.
In these cases, security professionals can use the same tech to find flaws themselves and alert others before criminals get to them.
This happened in the recent Java incident , as well as the PHP one - where there was a scramble to patch the flaws before they could be exploited.
These are not new - the world stood still in recent years as CrowdStrike and then Amazon Web Services ground many devices and systems to a halt.
Part of this may be down to technical debt - a term used when operators go for quick fixes to software instead of solving an underlying problem.
A build-up of surface-level fixes can eventually end up with more serious problems down the line.
With AI causing many companies to re-evaluate their cyber-security, they may be issuing more updates to patch flaws they have found.
Outages are often also a reminder of the physical tech our online world relies on - such as cables, servers and data centres.

As US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors.
On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.
The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.
South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market.

But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China.

This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress , external , a US-based think-tank.
China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests".

This is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips.

One of those is Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed, whose former director Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Calls for tighter export controls have grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang admited to an affair with her and resigned as CEO .

Megaspeed, the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia, is accused of illegally smuggling chips to Chinese companies after purchasing them for use in data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

The company has denied these allegations, defended its business as "legitimate and lawful", and said it has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". It also said Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director in late 2023 and left the firm last year.

The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, however, has said Brazil and the four South East Asian nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips that Washington wants to keep out of China's hands.

The new measures are aimed at ensuring sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the bureau added. Licences will be issued on a "case-by-case basis", it said.
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Batam in Indonesia is emerging as a major regional data centre hub

But ministers are inviting British firms to bid for the contract from 2029, with a procurement programme beginning next summer.

A Commons Committee had called on the government to part ways and appoint a company "more compatible with UK values". Protesters regularly target Palantir over Israel's use of its technology in the Gaza conflict and oppose its use in US immigration enforcement.
The £330m deal, which began in 2024 to help manage hospital waiting lists in England, was due to run until 2031.

The prime minister had faced pressure from some Labour MPs to cut ties with Palantir. They said they were extremely disappointed by the decision, calling the contract "an albatross" hanging around the NHS's neck.
There have also been concerns raised about how patient data will be used .
Palantir, which was co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, has interests in US defence and security, and has contracts with the Israeli military.
Health minister James Frith said the move was "not about the politics of executives of suppliers, nor is it about the territories or customers that one company or one supplier makes".
The government says UK companies will be encouraged to tender to avoid overdependence on one supplier.
The timeframe is not fast enough for some members of the government.
Dame Chi Onwurah, Labour MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West, said the government needed to "act urgently" to procure "credible domestic alternatives".
"The government should not wait two years, it must start reducing this dependency now," she said.
Former Labour shadow chancellor John McDonnell went further, and accused Palantir of "human rights abuses". He said his constituents in Hayes and Harlington "expect the contract to be ended".
Liberal Democrat health spokeswoman Helen Morgan criticised the company for what she called its "appalling human rights record, run by an ally of Donald Trump".

The British Medical Association, which represents doctors, said it was glad the government had shown it was listening to its concerns about Palantir, but was frustrated the process of changing to another company was further delayed.
Palantir UK said it was right to press forward with the programme which was exceeding targets.

"We are proud of our work to date to help deliver more operations, speed up discharge and reduce the time patients need to wait to find out if they have cancer," Palantir UK senior vice-president Tom Watson said.

Gamers can hardly contain their excitement as the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 approaches.
Grand Theft Auto fans have waited 13 long years for the latest edition of the game to be released - and going to extreme lengths to be ready for its launch.
GTA 6 will be released at midnight on Thursday - and Victoria Evans, from West Sussex, is not leaving anything to chance.

She has her alarm set for 05:00 GMT, and has a day off booked. She says she put the game's release on her leave request form which was approved, she told BBC News, despite the fact her boss "doesn't know what GTA 6 is".
She's far from the only one. For the game's launch day, HR software company BrightHR , external looked at absence data from more than 1.2 million employees from 70,000 businesses across the UK.
It found GTA was mentioned in 4.6% of time-off requests by employees. Throughout November and December, it said an estimated 83,000 days had been booked off for the game.
And booking leave is only one of the ways fans are making sure for the big day. Others are buying a new console to play it on or even pretending they're halfway around the world to get early access.
Market intelligence firm Sensor Tower estimates , external GTA 6 has already generated $1.18bn (£894m) from 12 million pre-orders - although Rockstar has not confirmed this.

Despite the option to preload the 212GB game, Jennifer Holmes, chief executive of the London Internet Exchange, said several UK internet providers including BT and Virgin Media had "increased capacity in anticipation of higher demand" ahead of launch.

When Red Dead Redemption 2 launched in October 2018, social media users were sharing plans to take the day off, with one analytics firm reportedly finding , external more people talking about calling in sick for it than any other game that year.
Similar conversations took place ahead of Cyberpunk 2077's release in December 2020, with fans discussing , external taking several days off to play.
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, GTA 6 is set in a fictional state inspired by Florida, which has featured heavily in the game's marketing, including this promotional blimp.
Some places have decided to lean into the trend for GTA 6 by offering incentives around the game - including the US Army's 3rd Infantry Division based at Fort Stewart, Georgia.

It gave some active-duty soldiers a four-day pass to play the game when it is released in November, as long as they sign a reenlistment contract for a minimum of two years between 1 August and 12 November.

"The idea was to have a unique incentives programme that connects to what soldiers are interested in," public affairs officer for the division, Lieutenant Colonel Angel Tomko confirmed to the BBC in August.

While Rassie Erasmus has run low of advocates elsewhere, in his homeland they rushed to his defence.

"Rassie was just asking questions," said former South Africa hooker Hanyani Shimange in the wake of Erasmus' six-match ban for a scattergun series of complaints about the injustices suffered by his Springboks side.
"But you have to look at the facts. Where was the accountability for that refereeing performance?"
Naas Botha, legendary South Africa fly-half turned pundit, described Erasmus' punishment as a "debacle". "You can't tell me they [officials] are untouchable," he said.

Supersport, which broadcasts South Africa's games domestically, published an article accusing Erasmus' critics of "pearl clutching" , external and "shooting the messenger" with regards to the game's faults.
Despite slurring the officials with a suggestion of match-fixing, Erasmus has the support of South Africa.
South Africa were ranked sixth in the world when he took over in March 2018.
He arrived off the back of a November tour in which they lost to Wales and were thrashed 38-3 by Ireland. New Zealand had racked up a record 57-0 win a few months earlier.
Erasmus turned the team around at speed, marrying their trademark up-front power with pace out wide.
They won the 2019 World Cup. The defended their title in 2023. They will go into the tournament in 2027 aiming for an unprecedented three-peat. And few would bet against them achieving it.

Long before the sport's data revolution, he was coding game footage, picking up the technique from a friend who worked in the military. He has since developed Outfox, his own software which allows his teams to run through moves virtually on a screen away from the pitch.

Tactically, he has also been ahead of the curve. He pioneered the use of forward-heavy replacement benches, giving his team an edge in the final quarter of the match. He saw the game-breaking potential of diminutive Sevens specialist Kurt-Lee Arendse and moulded Andre Esterhuizen into a genuine hybrid player, capable of playing in the back row and the backline.
Trick plays - forcing a scrum with a deliberate infringement off kick-off, or setting up a line-out in the middle of the pitch - have been part of Erasmus' arsenal.

There was controversy before the match against France last weekend when he made use of the Nations Championships looser regulations to swap his starting front row just over an hour before kick-off. Previously, he demoted himself to water boy so he could run the touchline during the 2021 series win over the British and Irish Lions.

Football issues correspondent Published 3 hours ago The Premier League's Key Match Incidents Panel has ruled there were six on-field errors in the last round of games - the joint-highest it has recorded in one weekend.
Each week, the five members of the panel assess all the contentious incidents and vote whether both the referee and the video assistant referee (VAR) have got the decisions correct.
You have to go back to the early part of the 2023-24 season to find the last time there were six mistakes logged.
The statistic does not include correct VAR interventions to fix errors, such as the red card shown to Brentford 's Igor Thiago.
In the last round of games almost every fixture had a contentious refereeing situation which was hotly debated.
It started on Friday with a potential penalty to Coventry City for a hair pull by Everton 's James Tarkowski.
Arsenal were denied a penalty following a VAR review after it was deemed Kai Havertz was offside.
Tottenham lodged a complaint over a challenge by Leeds United 's Jayden Bogle, who was not shown a red card.
But which decisions did the KMI Panel rule were incorrect? Some of the votes might surprise you.

Such was the controversy across the weekend, it may come as a surprise that the KMI Panel ruled only two were missed VAR interventions. There have been six missed overall, the same number as this stage last season.
Incident 1: Coventry 's Caleb Yirenkyi appeared to have his hair pulled inside the area by Everton 's James Tarkowski. No penalty was awarded.
KMI Panel vote: 5:0 incorrect, for the on-field decision and the VAR.
What the KMI Panel said: "Tarkowski had a hold of Yirenkyi's hair and the panel unanimously felt that VAR should have intervened."

Incident 2: Arsenal 's Kai Havertz was pulled down inside the area by Hull City 's Nobel Mendy. The VAR, Michael Oliver, sent referee Farai Hallam to the pitchside monitor but it was not given due to an offside offence by the Germany international.
KMI Panel vote: 5:0 incorrect, for the on-field decision and the VAR.
What the KMI Panel said: "Although Harvertz is clearly in an offside position, there is a clear and impactful holding action by Mendy before any potential offside offence."

When the KMI Panel sits down to vote there are two separate considerations.
The first is on the decision of the referee, which is a basic judgement in law and the Premier League's expected interpretation.
The second is on the potential VAR intervention. This takes into account what the referee has said, the available replay angles and the high bar for intervention.

England 328 (48.3 overs): Duckett 133, Jacks 59; Edwards 4-31
England confidently swept aside Australia in the third one-day international in Hobart to seal a statement series win.

At times the series decider felt inconsequential - the latest seismic turn in Australia's sandpaper scandal taking all attention during Australia's chase - but Harry Brook's side won by 97 runs in an important step as they build towards next year's World Cup.
Even when failing to fully take advantage of a fast start, England reached 328 before being bowled out in the penultimate over, with Ben Duckett making a fine 133 from 115 balls.

Duckett's century, after all of his struggles in last winter's Ashes, was his first for England on Australian soil. A 48-ball 59 from Will Jacks ensured his innings was not wasted as Australia's spinners slowed scoring through the middle.
Just as impressive was another exciting effort from England's new-ball pair Gus Atkinson and Sonny Baker.

Atkinson dismissed Travis Head for the third time in a row in the first over - something to be noted before next year's Ashes series. He also hit Cameron Green with a brutal bouncer that forced the all-rounder to retire hurt.

Baker had Australia captain Mitchell Marsh caught at second slip in the second over, soon added the wicket of Josh Inglis and also dismissed Green's concussion replacement Oliver Peake en route to figures of 4-45.
It helped England calmly close out the win and, after being dismissed for 131 in the series opener, their recovery is noteworthy.
Australia, meanwhile, have questions to ponder on and off the field - many of which are unlikely to be answered before a five-match T20 series begins between these sides on Saturday.

On the field, Australia can at least point to the fact key bowlers – most notably under-fire captain Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood – have been rested for this series as a caveat for their defeat.
On the evidence of this series, England, though inconsistent, look the more settled side.
England had taken strides in ODI cricket this year, beating Sri Lanka (twice) and India, only to be checked by their horror defeats in Pakistan last month. This corrects that course.
Duckett was impressive again but the most significant learning from this series may be the emergence of Baker in partnership with Atkinson.
The 23-year-old Hampshire quick was brought in after defeat in the first ODI and has added real threat with the new ball in his first meeting with Australia.

Bowling has been England's weaker suit in recent ODIs but, given another good start, Liam Dawson was again able to ease through his overs of left-arm spin, bowling Cooper Connolly, having Jack Edwards caught at short fine leg and taking Matt Renshaw caught and bowled with his second ball.

Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The 3pm blackout has existed in English football since the 1960s
Football issues correspondent Published 9 hours ago After 60 years, is time finally running out on the 3pm blackout in football?
With pretty much every available television slot now exhausted, next year the Premier League and the EFL are set to hold serious discussions about its future.
There are concerns, especially within non-league football, that removing the blackout could have detrimental effects on attendances and finances.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham agrees, urging caution and suggesting the health of the football pyramid should come first .
But many Premier League fans feel they are short-changed, locked out of many of their team's fixtures just because they live in this country.
Go anywhere else in the world, and every single match is available live.
With streaming so prevalent, to some the blackout feels archaic.
Yet it is a complex situation, and many feel the depth of English football's pyramid is like nowhere else.
BBC Sport looks at the history of the blackout, why it is unique to British football and the arguments for and against keeping it.
It is the start of the 1964-65 season and the BBC launches a programme called Match of the Day .
Highlights of one match would be broadcast on BBC Two, a channel which at the time was only available in London.
Yet some clubs were concerned. Would fans still turn up to games?
Burnley chairman Bob Lord was the first owner to refuse to allow the cameras into Turf Moor. At the end of the season, several other clubs tried to block the renewal of the deal.
A compromise was reached and the BBC agreed not to reveal the televised Saturday match until all games had ended.
Fast forward 20 years to 1987. With dwindling attendances across the European domestic leagues, partly influenced by crowd trouble, Uefa took up England's idea.
Each country could designate a two-and-a-half-hour "transmission-free period", as long as at least 50% of matches in the top two leagues were taking place.
This was "designed to ensure that spectators are not deterred from attending local football matches of any kind and/or participating in matches at amateur and/or youth level".
Today, the situation has gone full circle. The only leagues that apply Article 48 are England, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
No other major country qualifies for the blackout - because no other major country has a kick-off time that runs from the top flight and through the divisions.
It is a tradition that is unique to football in the United Kingdom.
Let's take Germany, often held up as an example of a country with excellent attendances despite not having a blackout.

This misses a key point. The Bundesliga has its own kick-off slot, 3:30pm on a Saturday, and no other division plays at the same time. The 2. Bundesliga, for instance, has a standard Saturday kick-off time of 1:30pm.

Elikia Mbinga dreamed of becoming a professional footballer and playing in sold-out arenas after captaining an Ajax side brimming with future stars.
But at 25, his life has taken an unexpected turn. Rather than showcasing his creativity on the pitch, Mbinga is making a name for himself through music.
He has become one of the most successful emerging afrobeat artists in the Netherlands, with more than 30 million Spotify streams.

It is a world away from Ajax's famed De Toekomst academy, where he trained alongside a host of Dutch talents who have since made their mark in the Premier League - from the Timber brothers to Ryan Gravenberch and Brian Brobbey.
It is clear the lessons Mbinga learned during his esteemed footballing education have helped shape his identity as an artist.
"As a footballer, I played in midfield and was a very creative player. That was my style on the pitch, and I try to bring that same creativity to my music," he tells BBC Sport.
"I want to experiment with songs, be as creative as possible and develop a sound of my own."
Image source, Elikia Mbinga Image caption, Mbinga (second from right) during his time at Ajax
By the age of 17, Mbinga was living the dream of many aspiring footballers in the Netherlands.
After impressing at boyhood club PEC Zwolle, he earned a move to Ajax and began a new life in Amsterdam away from his mother and seven siblings.

During his four seasons at the club, he shared the dressing room with brothers Quinten and Jurrien Timber, now of Crystal Palace and Arsenal, who joined Ajax from Feyenoord around the same time Mbinga arrived from Zwolle.

"We had a feeling that we had joined this journey together," Mbinga recalls. "We stepped in together. Already then, you could see that Quinten and Jurrien were like machines. They were built like machines from a young age."

He remembers the technical elegance of Liverpool midfielder Gravenberch and the physical prowess of striker Brobbey, who went on to score 56 goals in 163 appearances for Ajax's first team before moving to Sunderland last September.
Mbinga also had the opportunity to test himself against some of Europe's biggest clubs, including Real Madrid, Manchester United and Manchester City.
At one point, he even captained the group and saw little to separate them in terms of ability. However, their careers would take very different paths.
"In terms of talent, there wasn't really a big difference at the time," he says.
"Then, maybe two or three years later, Ryan Gravenberch had already made his first-team debut for Ajax. So it's all about development, right? And the same goes for the other guys."

Mauricio Pochettino has said he will restore Manchester United to being the most successful football club in the city.
The Argentine is scheduled to begin his new role as United manager on Wednesday after agreeing a two-and-a-half-year contract.
The United States beat Haiti 2-0 in Cincinnati in his final game in charge on Tuesday, after which he spoke to TNT Sports. , external
Analyst DaMarcus Beasley, who spent the 2006-07 season on loan with Manchester City, joked that "Manchester is blue, it will always be blue".
Pochettino replied: "No way, you will see. Give me time and that is going to change."
The former Chelsea, Tottenham and Southampton boss flew directly to Manchester on a private jet after the game and landed at around 11:30 GMT before heading to the club's Carrington training ground.
"We're excited because the new challenge is big, but it's the adrenaline that you want to feel," he said.
"We are going to have a different job but we have the experience to deal with that. We need to add our common sense in the way that we are going to approach all the things.
"We know that it is not a situation that deserves to be at a club like Manchester United and for the fanbase."
Tuesday's win ensured the US advanced to the Concacaf Nations League semi-finals and that Pochettino finished with a 62.16% win ratio from 37 games in charge.
The 54-year-old led the team to the 2025 Gold Cup final and the last 16 of the 2026 World Cup, when the US were co-hosts.
"I am proud of what we achieved," he said in a statement on Instagram. , external
"When we arrived, I wanted us to believe that we could compete with anyone. I hope today that belief is stronger, not only with the players but with everyone who supports this team.
"This experience has re-energised me and given me so much, both in football and personally.

"Leaving is tough at this moment, but sometimes in football an opportunity comes that is impossible to say no to. I have always believed in following my heart, even when it means leaving a place where I have been very happy.
"I hope this team continues to grow and achieves all the success it deserves."

Image source, Getty Images By Richard Winton BBC Sport Scotland You know Josh Kerr, right?

The guy with the shades. The fastest man to ever run a mile. Scottish, but with a curious transatlantic accent. Slicked-back hair. Beard. Usually got a medal of some kind slung around his neck. No stranger to telling you what he thinks.

That's Kerr the competitor, one of the foremost faces in world athletics, and a man who rampaged around London's Olympic Stadium in three minutes 42.66 seconds in July to set a new world record - then followed it up with a home Commonwealth gold and an imperious triumph at the Ultimate Championship.

Kerr recognises the description, smiling as it's articulated. But is there another version of him? Speaking to him during one of his regular returns to Scotland from his New Mexico base, it becomes clear there is.
There's scant chat about records, medals and his enjoyably niggly rivalry with Jakob Ingebrigtsen.

Instead, he talks about disguising alcohol-free cider, entering races under a false name, cold-calling universities, being starstruck meeting Scotland's rugby players and his granny keeping him humble.

This is the Kerr who spent the thick end of an hour on a chilly August evening taking selfies, signing his name and sharing his wisdom with young fans at Scotstoun after his Commonwealth medal presentation.
The Kerr who is still a regular visitor to first club Edinburgh AC's training sessions. This is Uncle Josh, who is heading for a party with his nephews after this chat.
"They really help me switch my personality into work mode," he tells BBC Sport. "I think everyone has a work persona and it's a bit more intensified when it comes to my sport.
"Not a lot of things matter when I'm focused on my job, but the rest of the 23 hours and 56-and-a-bit minutes of the day, it's very different."

Watch on iPlayer 'My brother still thinks he can beat me... that's the Kerr delusion' Kerr is sitting in the bay window of his parents' dining room as the autumnal gloom gathers in this desirable part of Edinburgh. All grand facades, imposing trees and permit parking.
His granny lives at the end of the road. His brother Jake and his family are 20 minutes outside the city. His school – the prestigious George Watson's – is a mile away.

The house has been home since Josh was five months old. Even now, this is where he returns on his five or six trips back to Scotland each year from his Albuquerque base, albeit the "chaos" of his teenage bedroom has long since been vanquished.

"It brings all different sorts of emotions," Kerr says of walking back through the terraced property's teal front door at the start of each visit. "As a kid, I would train from here every day. Everything started from that door.
"It's nice to fall back into that routine when I'm here. I can see the splits I'm running in my loops versus when I was 15. Slightly quicker..."

Former Spain midfielder Juan Mata has announced his retirement from playing at the age of 38.

Mata, who made 41 international appearances, was part of the Spain squad that won the 2010 World Cup, and he helped his country win the European Championship two years later when he scored in the 4-0 final victory against Italy.
A former Real Madrid youth player, he joined Valencia in 2007 before a move to Chelsea in August 2011 where he won the Champions League, Europa League and FA Cup.
Mata moved to Manchester United in January 2014 and helped them claim the Europa League, FA Cup and League Cup prior to his departure in 2022.
He went on to have spells at Turkish side Galatasaray and Vissel Kobe in Japan before he played for Australian sides Western Sydney Wanderers and Melbourne Victory.
"Football will never leave my life," said Mata. "There are so many ways to continue loving the game, so many ways to keep using it as a vehicle for development.
"I may stop playing professionally, but I will never stop being a footballer."
Mata was Chelsea's player of the year in both full seasons he was at Stamford Bridge. He made 82 league appearances for the club, scoring 18 goals.
At Manchester United, he scored 51 goals in 285 outings before leaving after his contract expired.
"Congratulations on a fantastic career, Juan! Everyone at United wishes you all the best in your next steps," said United statement. , external

The latest stop on Zinedine Zidane's homecoming tour was an important one for the new France head coach. When Les Bleus took on Turkey in Bordeaux on Sunday night, the ex-midfielder was returning to the city in which he spent four formative years of his playing career, between 1992 and 1996.

"I became a man in Bordeaux," Zidane fondly recalled in the build-up. France edged triumphed 2-1 with an uninspiring display, but it did not dampen the mood of the 40,000 fans inside the Stade Atlantique.

While the 1998 World Cup winner was not necessarily in familiar surroundings (the out-of-town stadium was built for Euro 2016, 20 years after his departure for Juventus), locals made every effort to make him feel at home, holding up a commemorative tifo before kick-off and chanting Zizou's name throughout.
Just a few miles up the road earlier that afternoon, Zidane's former club were playing their fifth match of the season in the sixth-tier Regional 1, in a north-western suburb of the city.
Thousands of Bordeaux fans had made the short away outing to Saint-Medard-en-Jalles' 3000-seater ground to watch their team seal a fifth win in five this season.
Girondins de Bordeaux, the six-time French champions, who were once regulars in European cups, now find themselves facing amateur opposition on a weekly basis.
Since 2022, the club has plummeted from Ligue 1 to the sixth tier through a combination of on-pitch struggles, mismanagement at all levels, and sanctions due to their financial troubles.
The club was taken over in 2021 by Gerard Lopez, who was previously in charge of Formula 1's Lotus as well as another French side, Lille.

While Bordeaux were already hamstrung by debts at that point, the situation on and off the pitch worsened under the Spanish-Luxembourgish businessman as the men's first team finished rock bottom of Ligue 1 in his first season.

A couple of seasons in Ligue 2 followed, before the club was docked down to the fourth tier in 2024. In their first National 2 season, they notably signed Andy Carroll but ultimately missed out on promotion.
The following campaign saw a repeat of that near miss, and the club was expelled from national-level football altogether this summer over their finances.

With Bordeaux left on the brink and whittled down to just eight full-time employees (down from around 250 a few years beforehand), Lopez sold up to Park Bench, a group of mainly British USA-based investors who also own Scottish side Dunfermline as well as a minority stake in Spanish second tier side Cordoba.
The supporters turned out in their numbers for the first home match of the campaign, which had been delayed amid the uncertainty over whether the club could continue running, against Stade Montois.

A bid to move the date of England striker Ivan Toney's assault trial to avoid a clash with Euro 2028 has been refused.
The 30-year-old footballer, from Northampton, is accused of headbutting and punching Saber Da Silva during a confrontation at a nightclub in Wardour Street, central London, on 6 December.

Toney denied assault occasioning actual bodily harm at a court hearing last month and a date for a trial of up to four days was fixed for 12 June 2028, which is three days into the Uefa Euro 2028 tournament.
He represented England at this summer's World Cup and has made 10 international appearances. It is not yet known if he will be selected for Euro 2028, but the application was made in case.

At a hearing at Southwark Crown Court on Wednesday, where Toney did not appear, his barrister Mozammel Hossain KC said: "It came to our attention that… there may be potentially a football match called the European Championship in 2028 between 9 June and 9 July."

Hossain proposed a trial date in August that year, adding: "We ask you please that the matter be put back to then for a trial so that if the defendant is included in this football tournament he can play.
"My knowledge of football is very limited but I am told he was included in the last one in 2024 and the England squad for the World Cup."
Judge Tony Baumgartner called it a "speculative" application.
He refused the request, saying: "It does not seem to me to be in the interest of justice to disturb the date that was already fixed."
The judge said the application could be made again if Toney is selected for the England squad.
Toney missed out on the latest squad for the country's Nations League ties.
Toney started his football career with Northampton Town and played for teams including Wigan Athletic and Peterborough United before signing for Brentford in 2020.
He scored 72 goals during four years with the Bees before making a surprise switch in 2024 to Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli.

Lauren Price has a shot at becoming Wales' first undisputed world champion against Michaela Kotaskova on Friday after the vacant WBO welterweight title was added to the fight.
The 32-year-old will go up against Czech Republic's Kotaskova in Cardiff in a fight that will be shown live on BBC Two and BBC iPlayer.
Price will defending her IBF, WBA and WBC belts at Utilita Arena and will now have the chance to add a fourth.
Mikaela Mayer has relinquished the WBO title before her rematch with Chantelle Cameron in December.
Olympic champion Price successfully defended her belts and moved to a 10-0 record by beating mandatory challenger Stephanie Pineiro on points in April.
If she wins, Price - who also holds the IBO and Ring Magazine belts - will become the first Welsh boxer to hold all four major world titles simultaneously.
Joe Calzaghe beat Mikkel Kessler for the WBO, WBA and WBC super-middleweight titles in 2007 but had relinquished the IBF title.
Price would be the fourth British female fighter to achieve undisputed status after Savannah Marshall, Chantelle Cameron and Ellie Scotney.
American Mayer held the WBO welterweight title but will instead go up against Cameron for her unified WBO, WBA, and WBC super-welterweight belts.
"As much as I looked forward to unifying for undisputed, it's dragged out too long and the Cameron rematch is now my priority," she posted on social media.
"No need to be holding up the welterweight division in the meantime."
Price was told of the decision late on Tuesday, and says it has added a further incentive as she prepares to face Kotaskova.
"It will mean a little bit more history," said Price. "And it just hits home a little bit because it would mean I'd achieved everything I set out to do in boxing.
"As an amateur, it was to go and win an Olympic gold. As a pro it's to become undisputed world champion. If get that win on Friday night I will have ticked every accolade there is.
"I've got the chance to grab that with both hands and I'm adamant I'm not only keeping the belts in Wales, I'm adding one."
Price faces a tough test against 34-year-old Kotaskova, who is the current WBF title holder and has not been beaten at welterweight.
Her only defeat in a 15-fight professional career came at the weight above, when she lost on points to Chantelle Cameron in a three-minute-round bout.
Kotsakova called the opportunity to fight for undisputed status "a huge surprise" that offers a chance to create history in her homeland.
In a warning to Price, she said: "It won't be easy for her. I have followed her career for many years and I saw in her last fight the first time there wasn't a big difference between fighters.
"Nobody's perfect; every fighter has some weaknesses and there's always a way to win. I see a chance."

"The picnic blanket that you'd happily sit on in Austin will get confiscated by security at Miami and will end up wrapped around you in the chill of a Vegas night."

Cadence Kim from Dallas lives the reality of being an avid Formula 1 fan in the United States, in the three diverse locations the sport now frequents. She will be among the 300,000 spectators around the iconic Las Vegas Strip this weekend.
Las Vegas joined the F1 calendar in 2023, a year after Miami, while Austin has been home to the United States Grand Prix since 2012.

Kim has put in the hard yards travelling across the Atlantic to witness F1 in its European heartland. Now she is reaping the rewards of owners Liberty Media investing heavily in the three US races, which have all recently been awarded new long-term contracts.
"Following F1 from the US used to mean accepting a massive barrier to entry," Kim explains.

"It meant setting an early alarm and trying to explain to room mates why you were yelling at 20 rich men driving funny-looking cars very quickly. It was more of a niche sport with no natural gathering places for a community to watch. What bar is open at that time?

"Having three domestic races has changed everything. It has shifted F1 from a purely broadcast experience into something tangible. It becomes a week-long experience where a fan gets to engage with a like-minded community, attend parties in the evening, and do a meet-and-greet. You can walk a track, sit in a grandstand, purchase the overpriced merch, hear the engines and literally feel a part of something."

Image source, ATX GP Club Image caption, The ATX GP club arranges watch parties for all races but when the Circuit of the Americas in Austin is hosting the US Grand Prix, the community arrives en masse

The community Kim is attached to is the ATX GP Club, formed in Austin by Maria Rodriguez and Julia Wezio, where watch parties help fans learn more about the sport and the drivers. With the longest running of the US races on their doorstep, at the Circuit of the Americas, she's ideally placed to compare all three venues for the fan experience.
"Vegas is a party," exclaims Kim. "The Nevada desert gets cold at night, so the cowboy hat doesn't make the trip, but socks, a hoodie and gloves do.

"Many of the teams have hotel partnerships so lobbies become team activation zones, and you might end up sharing an elevator with an engineer. The fan flow is well managed with everyone being funnelled through specific pedestrian walkways, but if you do have a ticket to watch the race at the track you are limited to staying only in that one specific zone.

Former three-weight world champion Jorge Linares remains in the custody of US immigration authorities in Texas and is facing deportation.
The 41-year-old Venezuelan was detained on Sunday when US Border Force and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers arrested him at El Paso International Airport.

"On October 26, 2023, he entered the country with permission to stay for a temporary period, but in defiance of our nation's laws, he overstayed his welcome. He will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings," said an ICE spokesperson.
"To be clear, a pending application or work authorisation does not confer legal status in the United States."
Linares is based in Miami and has fought more than 10 times in America.
The immigration law firm Wilner & O'Reilly are representing Linares and they denied their client was in the US illegally.
"Mr Linares is authorised to be in the United States and he has cooperated fully with immigration authorities," said a Wilner & O'Reilly statement.
"We are in communication with ICE and are working to resolve this matter as quickly as possible. Immigration matters follow established procedures, and those procedures take time.
"We are confident in Mr. Linares's position and ask his fans, the press and the public for patience in the meantime."
Published 1 day ago Linares posted a message on social media on Sunday saying that "ICE has me at the Texas border crossing. This is crazy".
He won 47 of his 56 bouts and claimed world titles at featherweight, super-featherweight and lightweight in a distinguished career which started in 2002.

Corporal Ryan Crowley has spent a decade helping get aircraft off the ground.
It has taken just as long for the winger to finally get his professional rugby union career to take off.
It was only a year ago that Crowley was plucked from his role as an avionics engineer with the Royal Air Force and recruited by Leicester Tigers.
The 28-year-old Welshman was handed a deal with the giants of the game, the 11-time Prem champions - when he didn't even know one was up for grabs.
"I thought I got sent up to Tigers to go and get experience and do a pre-season with a pro team," he told BBC Sport.
Chinnor, the second division side he was playing for, asked him to join Geoff Parling's Tigers for the early weeks of their Prem Rugby Cup campaign last season.
"After a couple of weeks Geoff said, 'you've been successful in your trial', and I was like, 'what trial?'," Crowley added.
"The silver lining to not knowing it was a trial is I had no pressure on me; I just came up and I was just trying to learn as much as I could.
"I didn't have any expectations of having to come out the end of it with something, but luckily I did."
Published 19 November 2025 Listen to the Tigers Rugby Show on BBC Radio Leicester
'I did think my ship had sailed - but I kept going' Crowley saw out the season with Tigers, playing seven Prem Rugby Cup games, and was handed a new one-year deal to remain with the club this term.
It was after that contract extension that Crowley was able to tell Parling what it meant to him to be a full-time professional after years of dedication to the British Armed Forces.
But through its elite athlete scheme, he has been allowed to step back from his role to pursue his playing career with Tigers.
"When Geoff told me he wanted me to stay, I said to him that for a very young Ryan Crowley this was a dream come true," the winger explained.
"I did think my ship had sailed - but I kept training and kept going."
Crowley grew up playing for St Peter's in Cardiff and had a spell with Welsh Premiership side Pontypridd before enlisting to become an airman when he was still a teenager.
At that point, rugby became something he did alongside his basic training at RAF Halton in Buckinghamshire and his studies in avionics, which took him to RAF Cosford in Shropshire.

For much of the next 10 years his focus was on carrying out maintenance and repairs on the sophisticated electronics on military aircraft - which has included Boeing C-17 Globemaster military transporters worth more than £250m.
And yet, his career in the military was never an excuse to give up on making it as a rugby player.

That's the message from Māori artist and rugby league supporter Charles Williams, who told RNZ the celebrations surrounding the Rugby League World Cup are about something much bigger than what happens on the field.
Despite the Kiwis suffering a big loss to the Kangaroos in the final, across Tāmaki Makaurau and beyond, supporters took to the streets waving flags, singing and celebrating their whakapapa.

At the centre of many of those celebrations was Williams (Ngāti Kahungunu ki te Wairoa, Te Whakatohea, Tūhoe, Ngāpuhi), who organised a series of parades to bring people together in support of the Kiwis.
The idea was inspired by the passion of Tongan supporters during the 2017 Rugby League World Cup.

"2017, the Tongan fans really took fandom to another level. So they went all out and they were basically riding solo. During that 2017 campaign, we saw them all over the streets of South Auckland, where I live.
"Post World Cup, I went to Tonga, did an art project over there, got to meet them and got to see even more the fan base there and how crazy they are.
"Come 2026, I really wanted us to kind of just get off the couch, really get out of the house. Let's be inspired by our whānau from Tonga, Samoa."
Williams approached New Zealand Rugby League with the idea and rallied friends to help bring the parades to life.
It began with around 50 people gathering at Māngere Bridge during the first week of the tournament. By the second week, the crowds had grown to hundreds, and the flags kept coming.

"I've noticed in this World Cup, there's been more of an emphasis on, yeah, hey, I'm from Tonga, Samoa, Cook Islands, Fiji, Papua New Guinea, so on and so forth. And even guys who are not a part of the Rugby League World Cup are jumping in.

"Guys from Niue, all of a sudden you got yellow flags all over the streets. They want to be proud of themselves and everyone wants to be proud of themselves. They want to stand up and go, 'Hey, here I am, here we are and we're from here.'
"And that's awesome, you know, and I love it. And I want people to really be proud of where they're from."
But the parades also prompted a bigger reflection for Williams about how Māori come together as a people, and how those gatherings are perceived by others.
Māori flags, including the Tino Rangatiratanga flag and He Whakaputanga flag, are often seen at hīkoi and protests, where communities gather to advocate for their rights, identity and rangatiratanga.
Williams said some people mocked the parades online, questioning whether supporters were protesting or taking part in a hīkoi.
And while he understands why people might make that association, he said the celebrations offered a different opportunity to come together under the same flag.
"One thing I've been thinking about for a little bit is how do we celebrate as a people? So we're kind of like known as the 'fighting people'.

"A lot of the comments mocking us were, oh, are you guys protesting? You know what I mean? And it's like, cool. "You know, I understand why you say that, because literally, we are always protesting. But it's been the first time, not the first time ever, but it's like the first time I've seen thousands of people with a Tino Rangatiratanga flag, happy, celebrating, and we're not actually fighting for anything.
"We're not trying to like get anything. It's just like, bro, we're just happy."
"We're under this flag. We're under this banner. And to celebrate, it's just been like, finally, we're just like, we're just happy."

The All Blacks say they're happy with the way hip and knee drop tackles are being officiated after Springboks coach Rassie Erasmus was suspended for criticising match officials.

World Rugby has banned the 54-year-old for six games for his post-match comments after South Africa's 21-19 defeat to France last weekend, in which he questioned whether officials were manipulating the game.
Erasmus, who has a long track record of publicly criticising match officials , believes they failed to notice, or ignored, up to 17 illegal tackles in Paris.

Hip tackles (a defender putting his weight on the lower limbs of an attacker in the act of bringing him down), and knee tackles (a defender starting the act of making a tackle while on one or both of his knees) was made illegal by World Rugby on 1 November.
All Blacks wing Leroy Carter required ankle surgery after being caught in a hip tackle during his team's Bledisloe Cup victory at Eden Park in October.
"The TMO (television match official) doesn't come in once. I'm not saying he's wrong. I'm saying if he didn't see it, it must be a technology problem," Erasmus said after the test.
"If he saw it and he decided not to act on it, is that not match-fixing? Is that not interfering with the outcome of a game?"
Springboks coach Rassie Erasmus will miss this weekend's test against Ireland.

South Africa Rugby has confirmed Erasmus will request a full misconduct hearing in order to "contextualise his comments and assure the panel that it was not his intention to allege that any match official had acted with ulterior motives".

The All Blacks also believe some illegal tackles went unpunished in last Sunday's 35-28 loss to Wales in Cardiff, with stand-in captain Beauden Barrett heard on multiple occasions asking referee Pierre Brousset about the hosts making hip drop tackles.
However, All Blacks hooker Asafo Aumua, speaking ahead of his side's clash with England at Twickenham on Sunday, said officials were largely getting it right.
"I think there were a few missed ones on the weekend, but that wasn't going to really change the result in the game," Aumua said.
"I feel like they're [match officials] doing enough, we've just got to be a bit more accurate in our tackles."
Aumua said he didn't think players intentionally made hip or knee drop tackles, but added they could be hard to avoid in a sport as dynamic as rugby.
"On the weekend, I felt like I'd nearly done maybe two [hip drop tackles], but not on purpose," Aumua said.
"I just got beaten on the outside and grabbed them and ended up swinging around, so I just let go."
Aumua said the best way to minimise illegal tackles was to focus on technique.
"Just getting in front [of the attacker] and trying to get them going back instead of swinging around."
As it stands, Erasmus is set to miss the Springboks clash with Ireland this Sunday and their Nations Championship playoff match the following weekend.
The ban is set to expire during next year's Rugby Championship, meaning Erasmus will be back in the hot seat in time for their World Cup title defence in Australia, which starts next October.

Three uncapped players have been named in the Football Ferns final squad of the year for a crucial two-match series against the Philippines ahead of next year's World Cup.
The Football Ferns will face the world's 39th-ranked side at Porirua Park on 29 November and 4 December.
It will be the side's last international fixtures ahead of the FIFA Women's World Cup 2027 draw in December.
Football Ferns coach Michael Mayne said the series was vital for their preparation for next year's global showpiece in Brazil.

"Once we know our opponents next month, everything becomes more focused and more specific, so these matches are vital in ensuring we're heading into a World Cup year with momentum and clarity about how we want to play," Mayne said.
The 24-player squad blends a heavy A-League Women's influence with Kiwi stars playing in Europe and will be led by Madrid-based captain Kate Taylor.

Rebecca Lake could be set to make her international debut after being named following her recent move to Central Coast Mariners. The centre-back, along with goalkeeper Brooke Neary, and midfielder Helena Errington are the only uncapped players named.
Neary, 19, made her first start for the Phoenix on November 6 when coach Bev Priestman made the bold call to drop experienced Football Ferns goalkeeper Victoria Esson.
Neary is among seven Wellington Phoenix players included for the series being played at the A-League club's ground.
The venue has become synonymous with women's football in New Zealand following Wellington Phoenix Women's historic run to the A-League Women Grand Final earlier this year.
The Philippines series was organised when the Football Ferns tour of Panama was cancelled last month after a 7.7-magnitude earthquake struck the central American nation.
"When you're building towards a World Cup, there is no substitute for time together as a group so we're eager to maximise every minute we have together in Porirua," Mayne said.

"We are in a phase where we're prioritising our identity together and the way we want to approach games and play that best reflects our strengths against what is a quality opposition with whom we've had experience with before at a FIFA World Cup.
"These are the types of games that will help me understand where we are in terms of the players progress and connecting to our internal priorities."

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/sport/2653426: Link: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/sport/2653426%2Fworld-rugby-right-to-crack-down-on-south-africa-s-agent-provocateur-rassie-erasmus
Analysis: It may or may not come as a surprise to many global rugby fans to learn that South Africa has a shortage of home-grown referees operating at the top level of the world game.
The nation is the home of the back-to-back world champions and the Springboks are favourites to win every game they play.
And yet, the men and women with the whistles are not coming through in the numbers that represent the extraordinary depth of playing talent 'Boks coach Rassie Erasmus has at his disposal.
Yes, that Rassie Erasmus - the one who has just been banned again by World Rugby under the organisation's "match official abuse sanction process".
His latest suspension is for six matches , including the 'Boks' next Nations Championship test against Ireland in Dublin on Sunday, and the following weekend's play-off at Twickenham.

World Rugby's latest sanction on the game's most prolific agent provocateur comes after his comments in a press conference during which he suggested some of the match officials overseeing South Africa's defeat to France in Paris at the weekend could be accused of "match fixing" such was their determination to avoid penalising what he described as the home side's illegal tackling.
Erasmus has previously been banned for criticising referees - most notably Australian official Nic Berry in 2021 after a defeat to the British and Irish Lions in South Africa.
In that case he filmed a 62-minute rant about what he felt were Berry's shortcomings and posted it on social media.
Berry, who described it as a "character assassination", has not officiated in South Africa since.
Erasmus and his South African Rugby employers have appealed the latest sentence and have requested a right of reply.
France wing Theo Attissogbe scores against South Africa during his team's recent win in Paris.

It is becoming increasingly clear though for all his protestations of innocence that Erasmus doesn't so much carry a rugby nation on his shoulders as whisk his many fervent supporters along in a permanent state of victimhood.

Erasmus can do very little wrong in the eyes of his acolytes; a quick scroll of social media will make that clear, although there is a sense among the more self-aware that while his complaints were valid his suggestions that "match-fixing" was at play may have clouded his argument somewhat.

It wasn't so long ago that Erasmus took great umbrage at suggestions by All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie that the 'Boks' occasionally went beyond the game's scrummaging laws to gain an advantage at the set piece.
"We're not f***ing walking around," was Erasmus' response in August after his team levelled the "Greatest Rivalry" series 1-1 with a victory in Cape Town.
"We're scrumming through. So, you know, we have never ever, ever been accused of walking around. So, I don't understand it."

In that case, according to Erasmus, the match officials were very much right to reward South Africa's scrum dominance and Rennie was very much wrong to air his opinion on a specific topic. Case closed.
World Rugby turned a blind eye or ear to the press conference "F-bomb" - there was no official response anyway.
South Africa are awarded a scrum free-kick during their win over the All Blacks in Baltimore in September.

But the organisation could not fail to act on Erasmus' latest outburst, although one wonders whether the fact that it came in the city which houses World Rugby's headquarters and in front of Northern Hemisphere journalists contributed to the urgency.

Photo credit: Supplied A 12-year-old Southland student has helped New Zealand snatch three world titles at the first aerobics world championships on home soil.
Organisers of the FISAF Sport Aerobics & Fitness World Championships say the event was a phenomenal success for Kiwi athletes and Invercargill as a host city.
The performances drew sold-out crowds to ILT Stadium Southland over three days.
Through five pregnancies, breast cancer and now into her 80s, Paula Barrett says it's never too late to start looking after your mind and body.
With an exercise trend towards weight training, especially for women, shoulders and lower backs are proving vulnerable.
Maureen Maclean says 16 years of regular yoga classes has strengthened her body and also boosted her social life.

Download MP3 5m New Zealand’s gold medal tally was headlined by Baxter Tamariki of Southland Boys’ High School, who won the cadet male individual section.
"It felt awesome just to represent my country. It felt really good to win it," he said.

Baxter said he had been training since February for the championships, juggling his other big love of rugby, as well as cross country running, middle-distance running, swimming, touch rugby, basketball and netball.
He said he focused on letting months of preparation show on the floor.
"I just like having fun, getting on the stage and just letting the work pay off," he said.
Baxter said he had been welcomed back to school with handshakes and compliments and was keen to defend his title in future.
Southland’s About Time crew - featuring Dani Kramers, Immy Morey and Billie Allan from Peak Aerobics - won the Adult Trio division at the championships.
Emily Lawn and Jen Beveridge from Christchurch's Game On Aerobics claimed gold in the Masters Duo - a win Lawn described as surreal.
"Hearing the Aussies get announced as second and the realisation that we'd done it and won was just indescribable," she said.
Beveridge lives on the Gold Coast, so much of their training was done by sending videos to one another, she said.
"A couple of years ago we joked about how we should do a pair because she has always wanted to compete for New Zealand and the joke kind of turned into reality," she said.
New Zealand Competitive Aerobics Federation president Sean Cresswell said the wins were the event's “icing on the cake”.
“Southland have been amazing hosts but also the experience for the athletes not only on the stage but off the stage has been world class,” Cresswell said.

The championships brought almost 500 athletes and coaches to the city, including a large contingent from the Czech Republic and competitors from Australia, South Africa, Belgium, Brazil, Poland and Uruguay, he said.
“It was great to see international world-class talent but also our own local world-class talent,” he said.
“We had our largest team that we've ever fielded - 88 athletes selected this year. We kept our standards high. The competition to get into the team this year was fierce."
Organisers were inundated with positive feedback about the event, he said.

Music correspondent Published 8 hours ago Harry Styles will make his Glastonbury festival debut next year as one of the event's headliners, alongside Sam Fender and Billie Eilish - with Cher among the other stars on the bill.
The veteran US pop icon will play the coveted Sunday afternoon "legends" slot, which is often considered a fourth headline set. It will be her only UK festival appearance of the year.
Other acts on the line-up include Sombr, Sienna Spiro, Lily Allen, The Streets, Chase & Status, Kacey Musgraves, Primal Scream and breakout pop star Adéla.
Tickets for the festival sold out in just 42 minutes last month , with demand particularly high after the event took a year off in 2026.
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Cher is bound to draw a huge crowd to hear hits like Turn Back Time, Believe and I Got You Babe
Electro pioneers Kraftwerk will make their Glastonbury debut with a headline set at West Holts - the festival's third-largest stage.

The event will also welcome experimental Canadian band Angine de Poitrine, who have drawn attention for their prog-rock sound and polka-dotted stage costumes; rap legends De La Soul and Mike D; and pop provocateur FKA Twigs.

"We are so happy to be coming back after our fallow year and, as we head into winter after that peaceful period, we wanted to give you an early musical taster of what's to come at Glastonbury 2027 with this spread of incredible artists," said organiser Emily Eavis.
"We can't wait to see you down here on Worthy Farm in June for some much-needed good times!"
The gates will open at Worthy Farm in Somerset to 200,000 fans on Wednesday 23 June, with music on the main stages kicking off on Friday 25 June.
Tickets prices are at an all-time high of £408, including a £5 booking fee per ticket.
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Festival organiser Emily Eavis watched Sam Fender's set from the side of the stage in 2022
Sam Fender will headline the first night, in what will be his second appearance at the festival.
He last played in 2022, immediately before Billie Eilish, and fought back tears as thousands of fans chanted along to hits like Seventeen Going Under and Hypersonic Missiles.
"Me and the boys have never been here before," he said. "We've never been here as punters, never played here before and we're doing that all in one day, which is the most crazy experience."

He will return as one of the UK's biggest rock stars, having won the Mercury Prize for his third album, People Watching, in 2025. Earlier this year, his duet with Olivia Dean - Rein Me In - became the UK's longest-running number one single of all time.
Fender is expected to release a new album ahead of his Glastonbury slot, which will land in the middle of his catchily-titled Proper Massive Stadium Tour.
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Billie Eilish was the youngest solo act to headline Glastonbury when she topped the bill in 2022
Harry Styles will take the Pyramid Stage crown on the Saturday.
It comes amid acclaim for his euphoric and athletic Together Together tour, which largely focuses on the understated dance anthems of his fourth album Kiss All The Time. Disco Occasionally.

Laura Brand read out the message on the disgraced comedian's YouTube channel on Sunday, in which he said he was not guilty of the offences for which he is serving a 10-and-a-half year prison sentence .
The message has prompted an official investigation into whether Brand broke prison rules.

The clip of Laura Brand has been played on outlets including BBC Radio 4's Today programme, ITV's This Morning, Sky News, LBC and the News Agents podcast. On Wednesday, Education Secretary Powell said the media should not have "amplified" his words.
"I was appalled at that [message] and actually I think mainstream media shouldn't have transmitted that either," she told LBC on Wednesday.
"It's a platform I don't think should have been amplified, to be honest."
Powell went on to describe Russell Brand as "someone who's not showing a jot of remorse, a jot of any sensitivity at all to their victims".
She continued: "This is somebody who's been convicted and found guilty of very, very serious offences and rape."
In a statement, the BBC said the Today programme had played the Laura Brand clip "in error, due to miscommunication within the team", and had since removed it from catch-up service BBC Sounds.
BBC News has asked the other outlets named above for a comment, as well as YouTube's parent company Google about its policy.

In 2023, after a media investigation revealing allegations about Brand, YouTube suspended his channels from making money from adverts for "violating" its "creator responsibility policy". But they are still available to view.
Brand's social media accounts on Meta platforms - which owns Instagram, Facebook and Whatsapp - were disabled last week.
Earlier this week, Downing Street officials described Brand's message to his followers as "clearly appalling", adding that it was being urgently investigated.
No 10 said it expects action to be taken if Brand is found to have broken prison rules.

Asked about the message, the prime minister's official spokesman said: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances.
"Prisoners cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments."

Joanna Page has said she was subjected to "really inappropriate" and "awful" comments from a fellow actor while on set.
The Swansea-born actress, 48, told campmates on ITV's I'm a Celebrity… Get Me Out of Here! that the unnamed male actor had whispered "awful stuff" in her ear before a scene.
"He just spent the whole time just sort of making up this song and chanting about what he was going to do to me, and nobody said anything," she told fellow campmate Mariella Frostrup.
Page has previously described feeling forced to laugh off being groped while filming with a "handsy" TV presenter.

Page spoke of the inappropriate comments during Tuesday's episode of the reality show, as fellow celebrities, broadcaster Frostrup and model Leomie Anderson, discussed navigating male-dominated work environments in their careers.
Page said the actor had come up to her "before you were going to do a take or something".
Image source, ITV Image caption, Joanna Page is taking part in the 26th series of I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here
Frostrup suggested that if she did speak up people would say she could not "take it", and would call it "banter".
Page then asked her campmates if they thought "we've changed".
"I think it has changed," Frostrup said, "because I look at my daughter now, and she just wouldn't put up with anything like that."

Page, who started out as an actress in 1999, previously revealed in an autobiography that she was warned about a TV presenter being "very handsy" and was groped but stayed silent because she did not want to "make a fuss".
She said she tried to keep it "light-hearted" and "would not have dreamed of making a complaint".

Reviews of the latest Hunger Games film have seen it dismissed as a "surreally awful prequel" and "a tortuous, costly mess" by some critics - but called "surprisingly strong" and "one of the best films in the series" by others.
The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is the sixth movie in the franchise, and tells the origin story of a teenage Haymitch Abernathy - who was played as an adult by Woody Harrelson.

In a one-star review, the Guardian called the film , external "overwrought and boring", and said it "has no actual interest and no authentic reason to exist, other than to gouge an income stream out of its fanbase".
But the Wrap praised its , external "memorable performances, intoxicating style and horrifying commentary", adding: "When the dust settles it may even be the Hunger Games that holds up best."
Image source, Murray Close/Lionsgate Image caption, Ralph Fiennes stars as President Snow
Sunrise on the Reaping is set 24 years before the first Hunger Games film, and 40 years after the previous prequel, 2023's The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.
"This prequel lands at some mid-point between Ballad and Hunger Games, which puts it on an immediately odd footing," Empire said in a three-star review , external .
"It can't escape the sense of feeling supplementary. It's an enjoyable-enough diversion, but essentially a footnote with aspirations."

Screen Daily called it , external an "underwhelming prequel", which "suffers from a lack of compelling characters" and "feels oddly incidental - a drab afterthought rather than a crucial new chapter".
Image source, Murray Close/Lionsgate Image caption, Kieran Culkin plays Hunger Games host Caesar Flickerman
The film's all-star cast includes Ralph Fiennes, Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace and Maya Hawke alongside Joseph Zada as the 16-year-old Abernathy.
IndieWire , external said Zada's performance is "charming enough", but "his character lacks the gravitational charisma or arc that, say, Jennifer Lawrence brought to the original films".
The movie feels "a little bit like a cold cash grab rather than a necessary deepening of the series' lore" and is "a dreary slog", IndieWire's critic wrote.

The New York Times , external also used the word "slog", adding: "One really misses the guiding presence of Jennifer Lawrence, who had the raw pathos to both ground and expand a world in a way many younger stars often can't.
"In Sunrise, we're instead left with fleeting moments in which Plemons or Ralph Fiennes (playing the evil President Snow) briefly elevate the film. They seem to be trapped in this dystopia too."
Image source, Murray Close/Lionsgate Image caption, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping will be released this weekend
However, the Hollywood Reporter , external was more enthusiastic about both the film and Zada's performance, calling it a "star-making turn".
Its critic concluded: "Sunrise on the Reaping is a return, after the disappointing Songbirds and Snakes, to the spirit of the first movies."

A former England rugby league player and TV pundit accused of putting her hand up a woman's skirt in a cricket club toilet has told a jury it "categorically did not happen".
Danika Priim, 42, has been charged with carrying out the alleged sexual assault in the toilets at Horsforth Cricket Club in Leeds on 22 July 2022.
Her accuser, who cannot be named for legal reasons, previously told a trial at Leeds Crown Court how Priim twice reached up her dress and grabbed her underwear.
Keighley-based Priim, who previously represented Bradford Bulls, Leeds Rhinos and England, including at the 2017 World Cup, denies one count of sexual assault. The trial continues.
Two of the complainant's friends told the court they also witnessed what happened in the toilet but, on Wednesday, Priim told the jury she was never in the toilets with the three women.
Prosecutor Chloe Hudson put it to Priim that there were only two alternatives – either she was lying or the complainant and her two friends were lying.
The defendant agreed she was not suggesting that it was an accident, or the woman had invited her to touch her, or it was a joke.
Priim told the jury she was never in the toilets with the complainant, adding: "I did not touch (her) in the toilets at all."
Hudson said to her: "What you must be saying is that these three got together to make completely false allegations about you."
Priim responded: "It's the biggest question I have – it's the why."
The prosecutor asked the defendant about how the complainant demonstrated to the jury how she was grabbed.
She added: "I'm also a very happy heterosexual woman. I'm with a man. I live with a man."
The prosecutor said: "The truth is that you sexually assaulted (the woman), didn't you?"
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Danika Priim, right, represented England at the 2017 World Cup
Hudson asked Priim whether she thought the complainant and her two friends had colluded in a "witch hunt against you".
Stood in the witness box wearing a chunky light brown cardigan and a cream-and-black scarf, Priim replied: "I believe they have."
On Tuesday, the complainant described how Priim "walked straight up to me and put her hand up my skirt and grabbed hold of my pants and my private parts".
The woman said she asked the defendant what she was doing, "then she did it again, grinning at me, and walked off".
One of the complainant's friends told the jury how she witnessed Priim put her hand up the woman's skirt.
She told the court: "I recall seeing her remove her hand, laughed about it and then repeated it.

Giving evidence on Wednesday, Priim said she only went to the toilet once during her time at the cricket club, and produced a photograph she took of her and two friends in there, to help the jury with timings.
She said she drove to the venue and was drinking soft drinks until later when she had one pint.
Asked about the police getting involved following the allegation, she said: "It absolutely broke me."
Since retiring from the game in 2021 Priim has appeared on BBC, Channel 4 and Sky Sports as a pundit, reporter and commentator.
