https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/emergency/267: Earth Sciences is working to determine the cause of wave activity that triggered a tsunami alert on Wednesday.

The National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) issued an advisory about 5.40pm, saying strong currents and unpredictable surges at the shore could be expected in coastal areas on the East Coast of the North Island.
It came after strong currents were picked up on tidal gauges at Napier and Gisborne, but with no sign of an earthquake.
No evacuations took place and the advisory was cancelled 15 minutes later.
Earth Science duty seismologist Sam Taylor-Offord said sensors initially recognised wave peaks of up to 30 centimetres about 10 minutes apart.

"Think about it like a fast moving tide. The height of that isn't going to inundate you, or drown you, or destroy a building necessarily but the currents that come with that amount of water coming in and out at that sort of speed are what is dangerous," Taylor-Offord said.

He said initial theories were that the cause was either an underwater landslide, caused by the collapse of sediments built up from river outflows, or the interaction of multiple swell systems against the coast.
Taylor-Offord said Wednesday's alert was a reminder that damaging wave systems could occur without storms or earthquakes.
"They can sweep in and they can flood things and they can pull things out with them.
"It could be a beautiful day and you wouldn't see it because the actual height of the tide in this case is not that large but the effect can be really significant," he said.
Taylor-Offord said readings showed wave heights peaked about 5pm, but it took time to determine whether decreasing wave heights were a lull or a genuine reduction in the phenomenon.

Youths at a Christchurch care and protection facility have escaped more than once in the past week after forcefully obtaining keys from staff.
On each occasion the youths remained close to the residence and were found.
An internal investigation is now underway into what happened at Te Poutama Ārahi Rangatahi - a care and protection facility run by Barnardos Aotearoa.

According to Barnardos Aotearoa's website, it is a "comprehensive, integrated therapeutic residential treatment programme for boys aged 12-18 with at-risk behaviour". They are referred to the facility by Oranga Tamariki.
Barnardos Aotearoa CEO Matt Reid confirmed in a statement to RNZ that over the past week "serious incidents" took place in the facility involving youths "obtaining keys through force and absconding".
"Oranga Tamariki was notified and also involved in offering ongoing support to Barnardos. Police were also involved and continue to support.
Reid said following the recent incident, Barnardos Aotearoa had focused on the safety and wellbeing of the youths and staff on site.
"Following our usual processes, we have an internal investigation underway."
RNZ asked how many incidents there had been, and how far the youths got.
In response, a spokesperson said the incidents were currently under a "thorough internal investigation".

"And part of this is to understand exactly what has happened. What we can confirm at this stage is that over the past week, serious incidents took place in our facility involving rangatahi in our care obtaining keys through force and absconding, and each time, they remained close to our residence."
Asked why they could not say how many times, the spokesperson said the statement was "all we are prepared to comment on at this stage".
Canterbury Police's rural area commander inspector Peter Cooper told RNZ Police had been called to the facility "multiple times in the last week".

"The nature of the incidents varies and include reports of youths absconding and assault. One instance reported on Friday, 13 November has resulted in a charge for assault and a 14-year-old will appear in the Christchurch Youth Court today.
"Police are aware of the ongoing concerns for the behaviour of some residents and continue to support staff at the care facility when required."
An Oranga Tamariki spokesperson said they had been notified of the incidents.
Barnardos Aotearoa said all youths who come through Te Poutama were "under the care of the state and have been referred by Oranga Tamariki for specialist support".
"Rangatahi who come through Te Poutama have faced complex and often traumatic experiences, many have lived through things no child should ever have to.
"Barnardos provides 24/7 care, therapy, and education to help those rangatahi understand the reasons behind their behaviour, heal from trauma, and develop the skills they need to thrive."

The New Plymouth District Council has voted to rip out its controversial cycleway after little more than a year.

At an extra-ordinary meeting, councillors adopted a mayoral recommendation to tear up the bike lane - nicknamed Tim Tam Alley after the shape of its concrete separators - between Morley Street and Belair Avenue over the school holidays.
Completed in July 2025, motorists complained of damaging tyres against the concrete separators, home owners struggled to access driveways and businesses bemoaned the loss of parking spaces.
Even cyclists were divided on its merits, some enjoying the security it offered while others felt it was too narrow and a few even had accidents after clipping the separators.
Mayor Max Brough, who made removing the cycleway a focal point of his 2025 election campaign , said he would be pleased to see the back of them.
"It's always nice to fulfil a campaign promise, but I think what's important to me is that the people who've been asking for this to be done for a long time have finally been heard.
"I didn't come here to make a big shout about how good I feel. I came here to do some stuff round town for people and this is just one part of many."
New Plymouth Mayor Max Brough speaks at an extra-ordinary council meeting about the removal of the cycleway's concrete separators.
It would cost the council up to $300,000 to remove the concrete separators and reinstate a painted on cycle lane.
The work would require approval from the Transport Agency (NZTA) - which installed the cycleway at a cost of $3.8 million - and was not budgeted for.

Council staff warned the elected members if the road surface was damaged during the Tim Tams' removal NZTA - which was not contributing to their removal - might require it to be resealed at an estimated cost of $1.6 million.
Brough said if that scenario played out the cycleway would be staying put.
"There's a contingency in that $300,000 for damage repairs, but if it fails drastically the work will be ceased. I am not spending a penny more."
His recommendation also included a provision for council to investigate the reinstatement of parking places lost during the installation of the cycleway as part of the long-term plan process.
This was an acknowledgement that reinstating car parks would require more design work as some earlier car parks might fall foul of new legislation requiring vehicles to allow 1.5 metres for cyclists.
Councillor David Bublitz - deputy mayor when the cycleway went in - wanted removing the cycleway also to be considered as part of the long-term plan.

"My new motion was around doing it all together. So, if we're going to remove the Tim Tams and we're going to put parking back in, because parking will definitely be part of it, we might as well do the roading markings all together. Rather than putting in the cycle lanes and then thinking about where are we going to put the carparks."
New Plymouth businessman Shane Devlin campaigned against the cycleway from its inception and helped collect a petition with 7500 signatures before it was built.
He gave a deputation at the beginning of the meeting and was thrilled with the eventual decision some four hours later.
"This should've been done a year ago. It's terrible it's carried on this long, but at least we've got some common-sense and we can move forward and get our street back again."

"I think the need of the community is far more important and I don't see how it's a problem for rates because they've only got so much to spend and they are not going to add 1 percent to rates just because of the Tim Tams."
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/emergency/266: A tsunami advisory issued on Wednesday afternoon has been cancelled after strong currents were picked up on tidal gauges at Napier and Gisborne, but with no sign of an earthquake.

The National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) issued an advisory about 5.40pm, saying strong currents and unpredictable surges at the shore could be expected in coastal areas on the East Coast of the North Island.
No evacuations took place and the advisory was cancelled 15 minutes later.
In its initial advisory, NEMA said it didn't know what had caused the alert, but said it was possible there had been an underwater landslide.
NEMA deputy chief executive John Price said there was no current threat to New Zealand's shoreline.

He said surges of up to 60cm on tidal gauges earlier on Wednesday evening triggered a notification to the agency, and the activation of the tsunami expert panel in addition to an advisory to civil defence partners that urged people in or near the East Coast shore to leave.
Scientists on the panel had since concluded the threat had passed, Price said, but something had happened.
"There has been no indication that there was an earthquake, but something has occurred that has fluctuated the tidal gauges on the East Coast, predominantly Hawke's Bay and Tai Rāwhiti, Gisborne."
He said Earth Sciences New Zealand was working to find out what was behind the waves, suggesting an underwater landslide or changes in the weather could be responsible.
Price said no mobile or public alert was sent out, with only emergency services, emergency management and civil defence partners receiving the "precautionary alert".
"One of the things is you don't want to activate the public where you don't need to, but we needed to make sure we were doing all the due diligence to ensure we could investigate what was happening.
"It's better to be precautionary and preventative than wait too early for a response."

Autism NZ spokesperson Kirsty Whalen-Stickley said what the mother said her son was subjected to was "completely unacceptable".

"It constitutes abuse and is not helpful for any child, regardless of what needs they may have. To put a vulnerable child in that position is horrific. I haven't heard something quite that awful in a very long time."
After the incident at Paengaroa School last Thursday, the boy's parents removed him and his older brother from the school.
But she wanted a public apology and for the school's principal and the staff member involved to be stood down.
"If [the principal] had just been accountable and actually made [the staff member] apologise to my child, we would have left the school quietly and happily."

It had been over one year since Megan was first told her son Elijah* presented with several features suggestive of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). He was on a waiting list and had not received a formal diagnosis.
She said that as a young parent, she felt unsupported advocating for her son.
She left her most recent parent-teacher conference in tears, and she had not been to one since.
"I left crying because of the way they spoke about my son. I understood their concerns, but it was harsh. Not one positive thing was said about him.
"As a mother, it's heartbreaking to listen to someone speak about your child that way. If you met my son, he has the biggest heart. He will go out of his way to help anyone."
She said this year, Paengaroa School provided Elijah with a teacher aide.

"She has been amazing, helping him to have more confidence and with socialising. She has made him more open to learning, and she's made him enjoy going to school. I cannot thank this woman enough. She has a beautiful soul. She has helped him in every aspect possible."
But she said even with a diagnosis, Elijah would not qualify for government funding.
That meant the aide was not with him in the classroom all the time, and Megan said she would often be asked to collect her son during the school day, when the aide was not there.

"At least every fortnight I'd have a phone call. They would tell me he's sick, he's tired, he needs to come home. I'd get him home, and there'd be nothing wrong with him, and he'd say, 'Mum, they just said I was being too much today, so they sent me to the office'."
Whalen-Stickley said that situation was so common there was a name for it.

"The colloquial term that gets tossed around is a Kiwi stand-down, and it's the idea that the child hasn't been formally stood down or excluded from a class but is regularly being excluded because the parents are being asked to pick them up.

"Every child has the right to access education, and if that is happening on a regular basis, it should be escalated to the Ministry of Education because it is common practice, but it is not acceptable practice. It is illegal."

Download MP3 4m As rain fell over Whanganui, several dozen people gathered to remember the lives of 12 people who died while patients at the former psychiatric hospital, Lake Alice.
The 12 are buried in unmarked graves at Aramoho Cemetery and the Whanganui District Council has on Wednesday unveiled a memorial garden and seat there in their memory.

It's now accepted that young people were tortured at Lake Alice's child and adolescent unit in the 1970s. The adult section of the hospital operated for far longer, closing in 1999 after almost 50 years.
As the rain relentlessly beat down on the sea of umbrellas shrouding the unveiling, Peter Manins reflected on why he made the long journey from Dunedin - to remember his "dear uncle" Frank Ginn.
"My uncle was a dearly loved youngest brother of my mother and her sisters and brothers. They were five, and Frank was the youngest of them.
"When he was in his early 20s, I think, he was committed to Lake Alice hospital."
The family thought he was treated okay, although they'd later heard about questionable practices there.
"As a boy of about the age of 10 and 11 I remember travelling here from Wellington, where my family lived," Manins said.
"We would visit uncle Frank and sometimes in the school holidays my mother and father would come up here and we would pick him up. My parents were teachers, so we had the school holidays off.
"Uncle Frank would come and stay home with us in Wellington for a week or two. He was always happy to go back."
Sarah Carson and Sally Anderon remember former Lake Alice patient Fred Emerson.
Sally Anderson was also paying her respects to a family member - her uncle Fred Emerson, who she thought died in the 1980s.
"As a family we're really surprised that he was in an unmarked grave and thought it was important we came today to recognise that and the other people who were in the same situation."
"He used to do a lot of wood crafts and stuff like that. He lived with his parents and when we went and stayed with them he let us help with that. He was quite a caring person."
Robyn Dandy is a survivor of the child and adolescent unit, as was her late brother, Michael. She's thankful the council's created a memorial.
"It honestly feels to me like there is now some sort of peace for them, hopefully, but it's just like they were planted in the place. It feels like it was a horrible thing to do to them."
Whanganui mayor Andrew Tripe stands next to the memorial seat.

Whanganui mayor Andrew Tripe is researching the 12 people's histories. He said they deserved to be remembered as individuals, and a seat was an appropriate memorial because it allowed people to sit and contemplate.

"It's doing the right thing for those who couldn't speak for themselves. The council and my role as mayor - we're custodians of the Aramoho Cemetery, and there are people here who have unmarked graves.
"They have an identity and they deserve dignity and respect."
Council parks team leader Lynn Te Ngahue and her team led the 30 people who attended the unveiling on a walk around the cemetery to lay flowers at the 12 unmarked graves.

"It's been quite profound for me. I had very little to do with Lake Alice in my lifetime and to understand what went on there and the recognition and the healing that's required has been really significant for myself and my team," she said.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/business/2663: Link: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2663779%2Ftragic-if-kaitaia-mills-deal-falls-over-northland-nz
Regional development agency Northland NZ says it will be "tragic" if a deal to save Kaitāia's two timber mills fails because of "delays caused by the election result".

Last week Japanese-owned Juken New Zealand announced it planned to either shut down its Triboard Mill and break it up for parts, or sell the land, buildings and machinery to a new owner who could restart the business in future.
Either option would involve the loss of 157 jobs by March next year.
It followed a decision by the company earlier this year to shut down its veneer-producing Northland Mill , also in Kaitāia, with the loss of about 60 jobs.
Northland NZ head of investment Tui Rutherford said a "complete solution" involving the two timber mills was still possible, but time was short.
Rutherford said prior to the election, the Government had been considering Regional Infrastructure Fund loans totalling around $30 million to keep both mills open.
However, the Government decided to put off the decision until after the election .

He said the investment package being negotiated involved not only an immediate solution to keep the Triboard Mill running, but also a way of bringing the Northland Mill back to life, creating jobs and making use of the high-grade wood grown in the North.
Rutherford said it had taken months to come up with a solution that brought together multiple agencies and connected them with local businesses.
"It would be tragic if the deal that was so close to being signed, falls over due to delays caused by the election result."
Rutherford said the proposed investment package would allow a New Zealand investor to upgrade the ageing Northland Mill.
The redevelopment would make use of the existing site, some of its infrastructure, and attract skilled staff.
Alongside the modernised mill, a second operation would turn waste and low-grade wood into woody biomass biofuel, he said.
"These two operations and the Triboard plant would expect to employ most of the workforce involved in both of Juken's Kaitāia operations," he said.
However, the window of time for saving the two mills would appear to be very short.
Last week Juken said consultation with the Triboard workers would end on 25 November and a final decision about the mill's future would be made by 1 December.
Final election results are not due until 27 November and forming a new government is expected to take weeks.
The caretaker government that holds the reins in the meantime has only limited ability to make decisions.
As reported earlier , a caretaker government was required to carry on with day-to-day administration but significant decisions were supposed to be deferred.
Anything that could not be put off should be decided in consultation with other parties.
Northland NZ head of investment Tui Rutherford says central government can still save Kaitāia's timber mills, but time is running out.
The Government's stalled negotiations to save the Kaitāia mills were revealed last week by Newsroom's Jonathan Milne .

Milne said the Government had been negotiating with one consortium hoping to buy the assets of the closed veneer mill, and with another - led by Wayne Brown in his role as a Far North businessman, not as Auckland mayor - wanting to buy the Triboard Mill.
Both consortia had sought government loans from the Regional Infrastructure Fund but the ministers involved deferred their decision until after the election.
Milne said the Oceania-Claymark consortium wanted a loan of 25m-30m while Brown's consortium wanted $5m.

The Hikuwai Bridge on the East Cape is finally reopening, nearly four years after Cyclone Gabrielle destroyed it.

The bridge is on State Highway 35 between Tokomaru Bay and Tolaga Bay, and was washed away in floodwaters in February 2023. It connects Gisborne and Tolaga Bay with the rest of the East Coast, including Tokomaro Bay, Ruatoria and the East Cape.
The community rallied to get a temporary detour road in place through private land owned by the Pourau Incorporation, and a few months later a one-lane Bailey bridge was installed.

"It's wonderful. It's been a long time coming but it's here now, so it's great," he said.
He lost all business for two months after the cyclone while locals rallied to get the bypass open.
"You take a big hit from those things so it takes a while to recover, but we're going to have a good summer. People hesitate over Bailey bridges and what not but it should be fine," he said.
Pourau Incorporation chair Philip Hope told RNZ it was a big moment to see the new Hikuwai Bridge completed.

"We've worked together to inform and support the cultural integrity of this bridge build, and it was really heartening the other day, we did a walk over just in final preparation, to see a school of mullet and tuna just swimming up the Hikuwai River... it was really special," Hope said.
The $50 million bridge has been designed so it can go underwater in future floods and withstand the force of debris piling against it.
Transport Rebuild East Coast project manager Richard Bayley said a lot of engineering had gone into the build.

"We've got quite a unique situation where we've got an old cliff face that's under the riverbed and on one side the silt means we've got piles 50 metres deep so the bridge is embedded in hard rock, and on the northern side they're a bit shallower.
"It's been quite challenging engineering... it's the strongest bridge built to the highest standard in our region. We're really confident this will withstand the test of time," Bayley said.
Hope and Cunningham are hoping other parts of State Highway 35 will also be upgraded.
"Resilience is still an issue on the coast - it's wonderful we are getting this bridge in and we are grateful, but there are many other bridges across our rohe that need to be replaced," Hope said.
"Roading up here has always been an issue so we just hope for a bit more love," Cunningham said.

Although both lanes of the new bridge opened on Wednesday, Bayley said it would be back to one-way traffic from Thursday so the Bailey bridge could be removed and taken to a storage facility in Hastings.
"It's time for that to come out so we need a little bit of room to operate on. Once it comes out we still have a bit of work to do on that side of the bridge below it.
"By Christmas it'll be fully open and everyone off site," he said.

Download MP3 12m New Zealand's main banks are joining forces in a new effort to tackle scams and frauds.
New Zealanders lose hundreds of millions of dollars to scammers every year.
Now ANZ, ASB, Westpac and BNZ have joined an intelligence-sharing network designed to help protect customers.
BioCatch Trust New Zealand will assess the trustworthiness of the accounts to which legitimate banking customers direct their transfers and payments.

If the network identifies the behaviour or characteristics of a receiving account as suspicious, it shares this intelligence with the sending bank so it can consider if it should suspend or investigate the transaction before any money is transferred.

Download MP3 2m BioCatch has been working with Australian banks since 2024.

"By establishing a framework for sharing this intelligence in real time, New Zealand's four largest banks will gain a better picture of criminal activity, and often, an opportunity to intervene before any money leaves a customer's account," chief executive Gadi Mazor said.
"Trust New Zealand will enable its present and future members to identify suspicious relationships and patterns that have previously remained hidden."
The network combines behavioural and fraud risk signals with selected payment and account data elements to identify potentially suspicious activity.

This can help banks prevent those types of scams where the scammer manipulates the victim outside of a digital banking session. Many of those scams reach their potential victims through emails, text messages, and/or social media posts.

It will take months to get the network up and running but as more banks contribute account intelligence, the network will grow more effective at identifying potential fraud, offering deeper insights and broader coverage.
Banking expert Claire Matthews, of Massey University, said it was a positive step.

"I think a collective approach is very helpful, because often something looks okay in isolation but becomes suspicious in combination. And stopping scams is more useful than identifying them after the event and trying to recover the money."

"Fraud and scams continue to be one of the top concerns our customers have when it comes to managing their money. We invest heavily in a range of measures to help keep them safe," Westpac NZ head of customer care operations Peter Barnes said.

"While big tech platforms continue to drag their heels on taking actions and initiatives that would better protect their users, banks are working together and with other parts of the ecosystem to fight back against fraud and scams. Our message to financial criminals is to stay out of the New Zealand banking system, because we're united and committed to defending our customers."

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/pacific/26622: Residents are being urged to "stay safe" and "be prepared" as Severe Tropical Cyclone continues to gain intensity as it moves through the Northern Cook Islands.

The category 5 system has been building steadily since Saturday local time, when it was a category 1. It passed near Manihiki and Rakahanga as a category 4 earlier this week, before strengthening to a category 5 system on Wednesday morning.
According to the Fiji Meteorological Service, the storm had maximum sustained winds of about 220 km/h close to the centre, with gusts up to 315 km/h.
Cook Islands Meteorological Service director Maara Vaiimene provided RNZ Pacific an update on how Xavier was moving earlier today.

"At the moment, the metservice office is working closely with Fiji Met Service in tracking this tropical cyclone, which as of 2 pm Cook Islands local time (1pm NZDT), is lying between Pukapuka and Manihiki and Rakahanga."
Vaiimene said the severe cyclone is moving in a west-southwest direction.
"Which means it will pass close to Pukapuka and Nassau, and moving away from Manihiki and Rakahanga in the next day or two," he said.
Earlier this week, a resident in Manihiki told RNZ Pacific that the community has been preparing for cyclone season since October, rather than waiting for official weather warnings.
Vaiimene acknowledged this, saying the northern pā enua [outer islands] have preparations in place for the cyclone season.

"One of the preparations that has been in place up in the Northern Cook Islands is they have activated their safety centre, and within the safety centre shelters, people can come together as a community and they can shelter until such a time that a tropical cyclone has passed by," he said.
He gave a message for families in and from the Northern pā enua (outer islands) as Xavier keeps swirling around the Pacific.

"The messages from the Metservice and Emergency Cook Islands to family members is to stay safe, be prepared during these times, and stay connected with your family members, either here in Rarotonga or overseas.
"If you are able to make calls, keep them updated on the current situation in Pukapuka Nassau during this time as a tropical cyclone passes by," Vaiimene added.
Vaiimene expects the worst of the cyclone to hit Pukapuka and Nassau will be tonight to Friday morning New Zealand time.

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/business/2661: Link: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2661800%2Fsmartphone-age-verification-arrives-at-the-checkout
In-store digital age verification is being launched with an assurance it will be secure.
"This is a simple call saying, 'Are they over the legal age? Yes or no?' And the answer's back," Kristy Gregory of Verifone said.
The multinational has about 90,000 Eftpos terminals nationwide that can now tap into the Government's digital wallet on smartphones.
"We're simply opening up the ability to use the credential now it's become available," Gregory said.

"There is a need. From a merchant perspective or one of the hospitality venues, it reduces fraud and increases security. And from a consumer perspective, it's one less piece of plastic that they need to carry around in their wallet."
Kiwi Access is one of the first digital credentials that will be available.
"Definitely for my stepson who rocks up to clubs now, he can simply use his phone to get in," Gregory said.
Kiwi Access, which for years has provided physical over-18 cards, has been part of digital ID trials with the Government and major Japanese technology supplier NEC for several years.
"New Zealand has established the foundations for a trusted digital identity ecosystem and is leading globally in this space," NEC's Steven Graham said.
"Kiwi Access demonstrates what becomes possible when those foundations are translated into practical services."

The overall system secures a person's ID using facial biometrics that sit in the Govt.nz wallet. It can then disclose what is needed to a merchant, for example proving someone is 18 or older at a pub or club, rather than supplying their full identity details as a driver's licence or passport might.
The Microsoft Outlook outage last week and ongoing security agency warnings about the hacking capabilities of frontier AI have raised fresh concerns about cybersecurity.
Gregory said the Government looked after security around the app and Verifone's part was tried and proven.
"We are simply the acceptance business... We've already got the infrastructure... we're happy to help.
"Our interface is highly secure... Today our network processes 700 million transactions [a year in New Zealand]. So we are a highly resilient, secure network.

"In terms of what is being passed through from the app to ourselves, there is no personal information. It is basically a call to Kiwi Access saying, 'Is this wallet credential registered? Are they over the age of 18? Yes or no?' That's simply all we're asking for."
Verifone recently introduced payment devices that can take palm or facial biometrics.
"The introduction of biometrics will require retailers to implement trusted third-party software," the company said.
"This form of payment is expected to start being offered from next year."
